questions.stem: A patient who fell asleep in a chair with his arm draped over the backrest develops wrist drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand the next morning, with triceps strength preserved. Where is the site of radial nerve compression?
options: Compression at the elbow below the lateral epicondyle
Compression in the axilla
Compression in the spiral groove of the humerus
Compression at the wrist near the anatomic snuffbox
explanations: Incorrect — injury below the elbow spares wrist drop and sensory loss of the dorsal hand, since the posterior interosseous branch mainly causes motor deficits distally.
Incorrect — axillary compression (e.g., crutches) of the radial nerve typically also affects triceps function, causing weakness of elbow extension, which is preserved in this patient.

Correct — "Saturday night palsy" refers to radial nerve compression in the spiral (radial) groove of the humerus from prolonged pressure (e.g., sleeping with the arm draped over a chair), causing wrist drop with sensory loss over the dorsal hand/forearm, but sparing the triceps since its branches arise proximal to the groove.
Incorrect — the radial nerve does not pass through the anatomic snuffbox as a site of classic compression; this location is relevant to scaphoid fractures, not radial nerve palsy.
questions.overview: Radial nerve injury findings depend on the level of compression: axillary compression (crutches, crutch palsy) affects the triceps in addition to wrist/finger extensors, while spiral groove compression at the humeral midshaft (Saturday night palsy, associated with midshaft humeral fractures) causes wrist drop and dorsal hand sensory loss with the triceps spared. Injuries below the elbow spare sensory loss and triceps function, presenting mainly with finger extension weakness.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old recreational soccer player plants his foot and twists suddenly while an opponent contacts his knee from the side. He develops pain and swelling over the next day. On exam, with the knee flexed and the foot rotated externally while the knee is extended, the examiner elicits a painful pop along the joint line. Which structure is most likely injured?
options: Lateral collateral ligament
Lateral meniscus
Medial meniscus
Popliteus tendon
Posterior cruciate ligament
explanations: Incorrect — LCL injury is tested with varus stress (adduction force), not with the McMurray rotational maneuver, and is rarely injured in isolation.
Incorrect — internal rotation of the tibia during McMurray testing, not external rotation, stresses the lateral meniscus.

Correct — external rotation of the tibia/foot during the McMurray test stresses and elicits pain from the medial meniscus, since foot rotation away from midline (external rotation) tests the medial meniscus.
Incorrect — the popliteus is not specifically tested by the McMurray maneuver and is not a classic structure injured in twisting knee injuries described here.

Incorrect — PCL injury is assessed with the posterior drawer test and classically results from a posteriorly directed force (e.g., dashboard injury), not a twisting mechanism with a positive McMurray test.
questions.overview: Meniscal tears often occur when the foot is planted and the knee twists suddenly, common in sports like soccer and basketball, causing pain and swelling that worsens with pivoting. The McMurray test evaluates for meniscal tears by flexing the knee and rotating the foot while extending the knee: internal rotation stresses the lateral meniscus, while external rotation stresses the medial meniscus, with pain or a palpable pop indicating a positive test.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of osteoprotegerin (OPG) in bone remodeling?
options: It is a receptor on osteoclasts that binds RANK-L to stimulate bone resorption
It is a decoy receptor secreted by osteoblasts that binds RANK-L and prevents osteoclast activation
It is a growth factor that stimulates chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plate
It is secreted by osteoclasts to stimulate osteoblast bone formation
explanations: Incorrect — this describes RANK itself, the receptor on osteoclasts that RANK-L binds to stimulate resorption, not OPG's decoy function.

Correct — osteoprotegerin is produced by osteoblasts and acts as a decoy receptor, binding RANK-L and preventing it from binding RANK on osteoclasts, thereby inhibiting osteoclast activity and bone resorption.
Incorrect — OPG does not act on chondrocytes or the growth plate; it specifically regulates the RANK/RANK-L osteoclast signaling axis.
Incorrect — OPG is produced by osteoblasts, not osteoclasts, and works to inhibit rather than stimulate osteoclast-mediated processes.
questions.overview: Bone turnover is regulated by the RANK/RANK-L/OPG system: osteoblasts express RANK-L, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors to stimulate osteoclast differentiation and bone resorption, while osteoblast-secreted osteoprotegerin (OPG) acts as a decoy receptor that binds RANK-L and blocks this interaction, inhibiting osteoclast activity. Conditions like menopause (increased RANK-L, decreased OPG) and glucocorticoid use shift this balance toward increased bone resorption.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old female infant born via breech vaginal delivery is brought in for a well-child visit. On exam, the examiner flexes the hips to 90 degrees and applies posterior pressure while adducting the thighs, producing a palpable clunk as the femoral head slips out of the acetabulum posteriorly. Which of the following best describes this maneuver and the underlying diagnosis?
options: Thomas test; slipped capital femoral epiphysis
Trendelenburg test; superior gluteal nerve injury
Ortolani maneuver; developmental dysplasia of the hip
Galeazzi sign; Legg-Calve-Perthes disease
Barlow maneuver; developmental dysplasia of the hip
explanations: Incorrect — the Thomas test assesses hip flexion contracture, and SCFE is a growth plate fracture in obese adolescents, not diagnosed by this maneuver in a neonate.
Incorrect — the Trendelenburg test assesses hip abductor weakness in a standing, weight-bearing patient, not applicable to a supine neonatal exam.

Incorrect — the Ortolani maneuver reduces an already-dislocated hip by abducting the thighs while lifting the femoral head anteriorly, producing a clunk as the hip reduces, not provoking dislocation as described here.

Incorrect — the Galeazzi sign compares knee heights to detect limb length discrepancy from hip dislocation, not the maneuver described; Legg-Calve-Perthes is idiopathic avascular necrosis presenting later in childhood, not in a neonate.

Correct — the Barlow maneuver applies posterior pressure while adducting flexed hips to provoke/dislocate an unstable hip; a palpable clunk indicates a positive test, consistent with DDH, especially with the breech delivery risk factor.
questions.overview: DDH results from abnormal acetabular development leading to hip instability, with risk factors including breech presentation, female sex, and family history. The Ortolani maneuver reduces a dislocated hip (abduction plus anterior lift), while the Barlow maneuver provokes dislocation (adduction plus posterior pressure); diagnosis is confirmed with ultrasound before 4-6 months of age, and treatment includes the Pavlik harness for younger infants.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old competitive cyclist presents with chronic buttock pain that worsens with prolonged sitting and cycling. He also notes he cannot sit on his wallet in his back pocket without significant discomfort. Straight leg raise testing reproduces his pain. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his symptoms?
options: Compression of the sciatic nerve by the piriformis muscle
Compression of the lower brachial plexus trunk between the clavicle and first rib
Compression of the common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck
Entrapment of the pudendal nerve at the ischial spine
Herniation of the L5/S1 intervertebral disc compressing the S1 nerve root
explanations: Correct — piriformis syndrome results from compression of the sciatic nerve by the piriformis muscle, often from overuse (cycling, running) or prolonged sitting, producing buttock pain worsened by sitting (the wallet sign) and a positive straight leg raise test.
Incorrect — thoracic outlet syndrome involves compression of the lower brachial plexus trunk and subclavian vessels in the upper extremity, unrelated to buttock and sciatic symptoms.
Incorrect — common peroneal nerve compression at the fibular neck causes foot drop and lateral shin/dorsal foot sensory loss, not buttock pain.
Incorrect — pudendal nerve entrapment causes perineal pain and sexual/urinary dysfunction, not the buttock pain and wallet sign described here.

Incorrect — L5/S1 disc herniation causes radiculopathy with pain radiating down the leg and specific motor/reflex findings (weak plantar flexion, absent ankle reflex), rather than buttock pain from direct piriformis compression of the nerve.
questions.overview: Piriformis syndrome occurs when the piriformis muscle compresses the underlying sciatic nerve, often due to overuse from running, cycling, or prolonged sitting. It presents with buttock pain aggravated by sitting (classically the wallet sign) and a positive straight leg raise test, and is managed with rest and activity modification.

questions.stem: A postmenopausal woman is started on oral alendronate for osteoporosis. What is the mechanism of action of this class of drugs?
options: They stimulate osteoblasts to increase new bone formation
They block RANK-L binding to RANK on osteoclast precursors
They inhibit 1-alpha hydroxylase in the kidney to reduce active vitamin D production
They are taken up by osteoclasts and inhibit their bone-resorbing activity
explanations: Incorrect — teriparatide (recombinant PTH), not bisphosphonates, is the therapy that primarily increases osteoblast-mediated bone formation.
Incorrect — denosumab, a monoclonal antibody against RANK-L, works by this mechanism, not bisphosphonates, which act directly on osteoclasts after being incorporated into bone.
Incorrect — bisphosphonates do not affect vitamin D hydroxylation; this is unrelated to their mechanism of action.

Correct — bisphosphonates are pyrophosphate analogs that bind calcium in bone, accumulate at sites of high turnover, and are taken up by osteoclasts, inhibiting their resorptive activity through various mechanisms depending on the specific side chains.
questions.overview: Bisphosphonates (e.g., alendronate, zoledronate) are first-line osteoporosis therapy that act as pyrophosphate analogs, binding calcium in bone matrix and accumulating at sites of high bone turnover where they are taken up by osteoclasts and inhibit bone resorption. Adverse effects include GI upset with oral agents, flu-like symptoms with IV infusions, and rare but serious atypical femur fractures and jaw osteonecrosis with long-term use.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman reports bilateral shoulder and hip girdle stiffness and pain, worse in the morning, with difficulty dressing. Strength testing is normal, and creatine kinase is normal, but ESR and CRP are markedly elevated. Which of the following is most likely?
options: Polymyalgia rheumatica
Fibromyalgia
Polymyositis
Dermatomyositis
explanations: Correct — polymyalgia rheumatica presents in older patients with bilateral proximal muscle stiffness and pain (shoulders, hips) worse in the morning, with normal strength and CK but elevated ESR/CRP, and responds well to low-dose glucocorticoids.
Incorrect — fibromyalgia is a chronic pain syndrome with normal inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP), unlike this patient's markedly elevated ESR/CRP.
Incorrect — polymyositis causes true proximal muscle weakness with elevated CK, not merely pain/stiffness with normal strength as in this patient.
Incorrect — dermatomyositis also causes true muscle weakness with elevated CK plus characteristic skin findings (heliotrope rash, Gottron papules), not present here.
questions.overview: Polymyalgia rheumatica is an inflammatory disorder of older adults causing bilateral proximal muscle stiffness and pain (shoulders, hips) worse in the morning, with elevated ESR/CRP but normal strength and creatine kinase, distinguishing it from the true muscle weakness seen in inflammatory myopathies. It responds well to low-dose glucocorticoids and is often associated with temporal arteritis.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with no significant past medical history presents with acute onset of severe pain, warmth, and swelling of the right knee over the past 12 hours, accompanied by fever and chills. Arthrocentesis reveals turbid synovial fluid with a WBC count of 80,000/mm^3 and a positive gram stain for gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Physical therapy and weight loss counseling
Antibiotics and joint aspiration/drainage
Colchicine and allopurinol
NSAIDs and observation
Intraarticular glucocorticoid injection
explanations: Incorrect — physical therapy and weight loss are appropriate for chronic osteoarthritis management, not for an acute septic joint requiring emergent treatment.

Correct — septic arthritis, suggested by acute monoarthritis with WBC >50,000/mm^3 and positive gram stain (here consistent with S. aureus), requires prompt antibiotics plus aspiration/drainage to prevent joint destruction and sepsis.
Incorrect — colchicine and allopurinol are used for gout management, not appropriate given the positive gram stain indicating bacterial infection rather than crystal arthropathy.
Incorrect — NSAIDs alone with observation is inadequate for septic arthritis, a medical emergency that can rapidly destroy the joint and cause sepsis if untreated.
Incorrect — intraarticular steroids are used for osteoarthritis pain relief, not appropriate for an infected joint, which could worsen infection.
questions.overview: Septic arthritis is an acute monoarthritis medical emergency, often caused by S. aureus or S. pneumoniae via hematogenous seeding, or N. gonorrhoeae in sexually active patients, presenting with fever, chills, and a single swollen joint. Synovial fluid WBC counts exceeding 50,000/mm^3 with a positive gram stain and culture confirm the diagnosis, and treatment requires prompt antibiotics plus aspiration/drainage to prevent osteomyelitis, chronic damage, or sepsis.

questions.stem: A patient develops muscle rigidity and fever shortly after receiving succinylcholine and halothane during surgery. Dantrolene is administered. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
options: Blocks L-type calcium channels on the cell surface
Antagonizes ryanodine receptors, blocking calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Activates SERCA to increase calcium reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
explanations: Incorrect — dantrolene acts on ryanodine receptors within the sarcoplasmic reticulum, not on surface L-type (dihydropyridine) calcium channels.

Correct — dantrolene is a muscle relaxant that antagonizes ryanodine receptors, blocking the excessive calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum responsible for malignant hyperthermia, thereby reducing cytoplasmic calcium available for contraction.
Incorrect — dantrolene blocks calcium release rather than activating SERCA-mediated calcium reuptake, though the net effect in both cases would lower cytoplasmic calcium.
Incorrect — dantrolene does not affect acetylcholinesterase or neuromuscular transmission; its action is directly on intracellular calcium release channels.
questions.overview: Malignant hyperthermia is a rare, life-threatening reaction to anesthetics like halothane and succinylcholine, caused by abnormal ryanodine receptors leading to excessive calcium release, muscle rigidity, fever, and elevated creatine kinase. Dantrolene treats this condition by directly antagonizing ryanodine receptors and blocking further calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old obese man reports burning pain and tingling over the anterolateral aspect of his right thigh for the past two months. He notes that the symptoms worsen when he wears a tight tool belt for work. Sensory exam shows decreased sensation over the lateral thigh, with normal motor strength and reflexes. Which nerve is most likely affected?
options: Genitofemoral nerve
Femoral nerve
Ilioinguinal nerve
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
Obturator nerve
explanations: Incorrect — genitofemoral nerve injury affects the cremasteric reflex and sensation of the anterior scrotum/mons pubis and upper anterior thigh, not isolated lateral thigh sensation.
Incorrect — femoral nerve injury causes motor weakness of hip flexion/knee extension and an absent patellar reflex, not an isolated sensory syndrome of the lateral thigh.

Incorrect — the classic isolated lateral thigh sensory syndrome from compression under the inguinal ligament is meralgia paresthetica due to lateral femoral cutaneous nerve entrapment, not the ilioinguinal nerve.

Correct — the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is a pure sensory nerve that courses under the inguinal ligament and is compressed by tight clothing, obesity, or pregnancy, producing meralgia paresthetica with burning pain, paresthesia, and hypoesthesia of the outer thigh.
Incorrect — obturator nerve injury causes weak thigh adduction and numbness of the medial thigh, not the lateral thigh sensory changes described.
questions.overview: Meralgia paresthetica is a purely sensory neuropathy of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve caused by compression under the inguinal ligament, often from tight clothing, obesity, or pregnancy. It presents with burning pain, paresthesia, and hypoesthesia over the outer thigh without motor weakness, since the nerve carries no motor fibers.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man presents with low back pain radiating down the back of his right leg after lifting a heavy box. On exam, he has weakness of plantar flexion and cannot stand on his toes on the affected side. The ankle reflex is absent. Which of the following best localizes the level of disc herniation?
options: L2/L3 disc herniation affecting the femoral nerve
L5/S1 disc herniation affecting the S1 nerve root
L3/L4 disc herniation affecting the obturator nerve
L4/L5 disc herniation affecting the L5 nerve root
T12/L1 disc herniation affecting the iliohypogastric nerve
explanations: Incorrect — L2/L3/L4 radiculopathy affects the femoral nerve, causing anterior thigh/knee pain, weak hip flexion/knee extension, and a reduced patellar (not ankle) reflex.

Correct — L5/S1 disc herniation affects the S1 nerve root (via the tibial nerve), causing pain down the back of the leg, weakness of plantar flexion, difficulty standing on toes, and loss of the ankle reflex, exactly as described.
Incorrect — the obturator nerve arises from L2-L4 and causes weak thigh adduction and medial thigh numbness, not posterior leg symptoms with absent ankle reflex.
Incorrect — L5 radiculopathy from L4/L5 herniation causes weak dorsiflexion and difficulty walking on heels, not the weak plantar flexion and absent ankle reflex described here.
Incorrect — the iliohypogastric nerve (T12-L1) provides sensation to the suprapubic region and motor to abdominal wall muscles, unrelated to leg pain and ankle reflex loss.
questions.overview: Lumbar radiculopathy from herniated discs most commonly affects the L5 nerve root (L4/L5 herniation, causing weak dorsiflexion and difficulty heel-walking) or the S1 nerve root (L5/S1 herniation, causing weak plantar flexion, difficulty toe-walking, and loss of the ankle reflex). Higher lumbar disc herniations (L2-L4) instead affect the femoral nerve, causing anterior thigh pain and a diminished patellar reflex.

questions.stem: A young man punches a wall with a closed fist and presents with pain and swelling at the base of his fifth finger with limited hand movement. X-ray shows a fracture at the neck of the fifth metacarpal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Buddy taping to an adjacent finger and avoidance of weight-bearing activities
Long-arm cast immobilization for 8 weeks
Immediate physical therapy without immobilization
Emergency surgical fixation
explanations: Correct — a boxer's fracture (metacarpal neck fracture, most often of the fifth metacarpal) from a direct impact with a closed fist is typically treated conservatively with buddy taping to an adjacent finger, avoidance of weight-bearing activities, and pain management with cold compresses.
Incorrect — prolonged long-arm casting is not indicated for this distal hand fracture; simpler buddy taping is the typical approach.
Incorrect — some period of protection/immobilization (buddy taping) is appropriate initially, rather than immediate unrestricted physical therapy.
Incorrect — emergency surgical fixation is not the standard initial treatment for an uncomplicated boxer's fracture, which usually heals well with conservative management.
questions.overview: A boxer's fracture is a fracture of the metacarpal neck, most often the fifth metacarpal, caused by direct impact with a closed fist, presenting with pain and swelling at the base of the affected finger and limited movement. Treatment is typically conservative with buddy taping to an adjacent finger, avoidance of weight-bearing activities, and pain management with cold compresses.

questions.stem: A postural muscle of the spine relies heavily on sustained low-level contraction and resistance to fatigue. Which fiber type predominates in this muscle?
options: Type II (fast-twitch) fibers, with abundant glycogen and glycolytic enzymes
Type II fibers, with abundant myoglobin and mitochondria
Type I fibers, with few mitochondria and primarily glycolytic metabolism
Type I (slow-twitch) fibers, with abundant myoglobin and mitochondria
explanations: Incorrect — Type II (fast-twitch, white) fibers primarily use glycolysis and glycogen stores, fatigue more quickly, and are suited for rapid, brief contractions (e.g., eye muscles), not sustained postural tone.
Incorrect — Type II fibers are characterized by fewer mitochondria and less myoglobin, not abundant amounts as in Type I fibers.
Incorrect — Type I fibers actually have abundant mitochondria and rely on oxidative metabolism, not few mitochondria with primarily glycolytic metabolism as stated.

Correct — Type I (slow-twitch, red) fibers contain abundant myoglobin and mitochondria, favor oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid metabolism, and resist fatigue, making them predominant in postural muscles requiring sustained tone.
questions.overview: Skeletal muscle fibers are classified as Type I (slow-twitch, red) fibers, rich in myoglobin and mitochondria, favoring oxidative phosphorylation and fatigue resistance, ideal for sustained postural muscles, versus Type II (fast-twitch, white) fibers, which rely on glycolysis and glycogen stores for rapid but fatigable contractions, as seen in eye muscles. Most muscles contain a mixture of both fiber types.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with several months of dull knee pain. X-ray reveals a lytic lesion with a "soap bubble" appearance located in the epiphysis of the distal femur, extending to the subchondral bone. Biopsy shows numerous multinucleated giant cells resembling osteoclasts admixed with mononuclear stromal cells. Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of this tumor?
options: Chondrocytes proliferate abnormally, forming a cartilage cap over a bony stalk
Stromal cells express high levels of RANK-L, driving osteoclast activity within the tumor
Fusion of EWSR1 and FLI1 genes drives proliferation of primitive neuroectodermal cells
APC gene mutation leads to osteoma formation in the skull
Malignant osteoblasts produce disorganized osteoid, lifting the periosteum
explanations: Incorrect — this describes osteochondroma, a benign cartilage-capped bony projection arising at the metaphysis near the growth plate, not the epiphyseal giant cell tumor described.

Correct — giant cell tumor (osteoclastoma) stromal tumor cells express high levels of RANK-L, driving osteoclast activity and formation of the characteristic multinucleated giant cells; it typically occurs in the epiphysis, classically at the knee, with a soap bubble X-ray appearance.
Incorrect — this describes Ewing sarcoma, involving small round blue cells and the EWSR1-FLI1 translocation, occurring in the diaphysis, not this epiphyseal giant cell lesion.
Incorrect — this describes Gardner syndrome-associated osteomas, unrelated to the epiphyseal giant cell lesion with soap-bubble appearance described here.
Incorrect — this describes osteosarcoma, a malignant tumor of osteoblasts with pleomorphic cells and irregular osteoid, occurring in the metaphysis, not an epiphyseal giant cell tumor.
questions.overview: Giant cell tumor of bone (osteoclastoma) is a usually benign but locally aggressive tumor occurring in the epiphysis, most commonly at the knee (distal femur/proximal tibia), producing a characteristic soap bubble appearance on X-ray. Stromal tumor cells express high RANK-L, recruiting and activating osteoclasts to form the multinucleated giant cells that give the tumor its name.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with chronic knee pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest undergoes arthrocentesis showing a WBC count of 800/mm^3. X-ray shows joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, and osteophytes. Which of the following best characterizes this condition?
options: A crystal-induced arthritis from monosodium urate deposition
A non-inflammatory arthritis caused by chondrocyte-driven cartilage breakdown
A bacterial infection requiring emergent drainage
An autoimmune inflammatory arthritis with pannus formation
explanations: Incorrect — gout also has synovial WBC in the 2,000-50,000/mm^3 range with monosodium urate crystals, higher than this patient's count, and does not typically show the X-ray triad described.

Correct — osteoarthritis is a non-inflammatory arthritis (synovial WBC 200-2000/mm^3) caused by abnormal chondrocytes proliferating and secreting proteases/cytokines that break down hyaline cartilage, producing the classic X-ray triad of joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, and osteophytes.
Incorrect — septic arthritis has a synovial WBC typically greater than 50,000/mm^3 and requires emergent drainage; this patient's much lower WBC count is inconsistent with infection.

Incorrect — rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition with much higher synovial WBC counts (2,000-50,000/mm^3) and different systemic features, not matching this patient's low WBC count and mechanical symptom pattern.
questions.overview: Osteoarthritis is a non-inflammatory arthritis from hyaline cartilage breakdown driven by proliferating chondrocytes that secrete proteases and cytokines, with synovial fluid WBC typically 200-2000/mm^3. Classic X-ray findings include joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes, and subchondral cysts, and pain classically worsens with joint use and improves with rest.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old presents with a painful, enlarging mass in the diaphysis of the femur with an "onion skin" periosteal reaction on X-ray. Biopsy shows sheets of small round blue cells. Genetic testing is most likely to reveal which of the following?
options: Mutation in the RB1 gene
Fusion of EWSR1 and FLI1 genes on chromosomes 22 and 11
Mutation in the FGFR3 gene
Mutation in the APC gene
explanations: Incorrect — RB1 mutation (familial retinoblastoma) is associated with increased risk of osteosarcoma, not Ewing sarcoma.

Correct — approximately 85% of Ewing sarcoma cases are associated with a translocation fusing the EWSR1 gene (chromosome 22) to the FLI1 gene (chromosome 11), detectable by FISH, consistent with this diaphyseal small round blue cell tumor with onion-skin periosteal reaction.
Incorrect — FGFR3 mutation causes achondroplasia, a skeletal dysplasia unrelated to this malignant bone tumor.
Incorrect — APC gene mutation causes familial adenomatous polyposis and its variant Gardner syndrome (associated with osteomas), not Ewing sarcoma.
questions.overview: Ewing sarcoma is an aggressive malignant bone tumor of undifferentiated neuroectodermal cells, occurring most often in the diaphysis of long bones in patients under 20 years old. About 85% of cases harbor a characteristic EWSR1-FLI1 gene fusion from a t(11;22) translocation, and histology shows sheets of small round blue cells with an onion skin periosteal reaction on imaging.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy is found to have an incidental slow-growing, stalk-like bony projection capped with cartilage near the metaphysis of his distal femur. Which of the following best describes this lesion?
options: Most common benign bone tumor, arising from the growth plate
Malignant tumor of osteoblasts with Codman triangle on X-ray
Fluid-filled cyst with fibrous lining found in the metaphysis
Undifferentiated small round blue cell tumor with onion-skin periosteal reaction
explanations: Correct — osteochondroma is the most common benign bone tumor, a cartilage-capped bony projection (exostosis) arising from the growth plate at the metaphysis, more common in males, and treated with simple excision if symptomatic.
Incorrect — this describes osteosarcoma, a malignant tumor with Codman triangle/sunburst pattern, distinct from the benign cartilage-capped lesion described.
Incorrect — this describes a simple (unicameral) bone cyst, a fluid-filled lesion without a cartilage cap, distinct from osteochondroma.
Incorrect — this describes Ewing sarcoma, a diaphyseal malignant tumor with onion-skin periosteal reaction, not the described benign metaphyseal lesion.
questions.overview: Osteochondroma is the most common benign bone tumor, a slow-growing cartilage-capped bony projection arising from the growth plate at the metaphysis, typically in adolescent males. It stops growing when the growth plate closes and rarely undergoes malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with multiple colonic polyps is found to have painless, palpable bony growths on his skull. Genetic testing reveals an APC gene mutation. Which of the following best describes the bony lesions?
options: Osteomas
Giant cell tumors
Osteochondromas
Osteosarcomas
explanations: Correct — Gardner syndrome, a variant of familial adenomatous polyposis caused by APC gene mutations, is associated with osteomas (benign bone growths), usually in the skull or mandible, that are often painless and palpable and may precede colonic symptoms.
Incorrect — giant cell tumors occur in the epiphysis of long bones and are unrelated to APC mutations or Gardner syndrome.
Incorrect — osteochondromas are cartilage-capped bony projections at the metaphysis of long bones, unrelated to Gardner syndrome or APC mutations.
Incorrect — osteosarcomas are malignant tumors associated with Rb and p53 mutations or Paget's disease, not the benign skull lesions of Gardner syndrome.
questions.overview: Gardner syndrome is a variant of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) caused by APC gene mutations, featuring colonic polyps along with extra-colonic manifestations including osteomas, typically in the skull or mandible. These osteomas are usually painless and palpable and may be detected before the onset of colonic symptoms.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman falls from standing height and sustains a wrist fracture. She has no history of major trauma. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) of the hip shows a T-score of -2.8. Which of the following best describes her diagnosis and the meaning of this T-score?
options: Paget's disease; focal area of increased bone turnover
Osteomalacia; defective mineralization of osteoid matrix
Osteopenia; bone mineral density between 1.0 and 2.5 standard deviations below a young healthy adult
Osteopetrosis; defective osteoclast activity causing increased bone density
Osteoporosis; bone mineral density 2.5 or more standard deviations below a young healthy adult
explanations: Incorrect — Paget's disease is a focal disorder of excessive bone remodeling with a characteristic mosaic bone pattern and elevated alkaline phosphatase, not diagnosed by a T-score.

Incorrect — osteomalacia is a defect in mineralization of osteoid due to vitamin D or calcium deficiency, diagnosed by pseudofractures/Looser zones and abnormal calcium/PTH/phosphate labs, not by DXA T-score criteria alone.

Incorrect — osteopenia corresponds to a T-score between -1.0 and -2.5, a less severe reduction in bone density than this patient's -2.8, and does not by itself confirm the diagnosis given her fragility fracture.
Incorrect — osteopetrosis is a rare disorder of defective osteoclast activity causing increased (not decreased) bone density, the opposite of what is described by this patient's low T-score.

Correct — a T-score of -2.5 or lower defines osteoporosis, and combined with her fragility fracture (fall from standing height), this confirms the diagnosis of markedly decreased bone mass with increased fracture risk.
questions.overview: Osteoporosis is defined by a DXA T-score of -2.5 or lower, reflecting markedly decreased bone mass compared to a healthy young adult, and can also be diagnosed by a fragility fracture (fall from standing height or less) at sites like the hip, spine, wrist, or humerus. Osteopenia (T-score -1.0 to -2.5) represents a milder reduction in bone density, and screening DXA is recommended for women over 65.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with an iron overload disorder presents with joint pain and minimal swelling. Which joint is most commonly involved in this arthropathy?
options: First carpometacarpal joint
Metacarpophalangeal joints
Proximal interphalangeal joints only
Distal interphalangeal joints
explanations: Incorrect — the first carpometacarpal joint is a classic site for osteoarthritis, not hemochromatosis arthropathy.

Correct — hemochromatosis arthropathy most commonly involves the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, typically presenting with pain and minimal swelling in a younger patient with elevated serum ferritin.
Incorrect — PIP involvement (Bouchard's nodes) is associated with osteoarthritis, not the classic MCP-predominant pattern of hemochromatosis.
Incorrect — DIP joint involvement (Heberden's nodes) is characteristic of osteoarthritis, not hemochromatosis arthropathy.
questions.overview: Hemochromatosis, an iron overload disorder, can present with arthritis most commonly involving the MCP joints, often with pain but minimal swelling in a younger patient. This distribution helps distinguish it from osteoarthritis, which classically spares the MCP joints and instead affects the DIP, PIP, and first CMC joints.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old obese woman who stands for long periods at work reports stabbing heel pain that is worst with her first steps in the morning and improves somewhat with continued activity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Iliotibial band syndrome
Plantar fasciitis
Tarsal tunnel syndrome
Medial tibial stress syndrome
explanations: Incorrect — iliotibial band syndrome causes lateral knee pain from friction against the lateral femoral epicondyle, not heel pain.

Correct — plantar fasciitis is inflammation of the plantar aponeurosis, associated with obesity and prolonged standing, presenting with stabbing heel pain that is worst after periods of inactivity (e.g., first steps in the morning) and tenderness at the base of the heel.

Incorrect — tarsal tunnel syndrome (distal tibial nerve compression) causes sensory symptoms on the sole of the foot, but is not specifically characterized by the classic morning stabbing pain pattern of plantar fasciitis.
Incorrect — medial tibial stress syndrome (shin splints) causes pain in the lower shin from overuse (e.g., running), not stabbing heel pain worse in the morning.
questions.overview: Plantar fasciitis is inflammation of the plantar aponeurosis, associated with risk factors including obesity, prolonged standing, jumping, and flat feet, and classically presents as stabbing heel pain that is worse after periods of inactivity, such as the first steps in the morning. Heel spurs often coexist, and treatment includes rest, ice, NSAIDs, proper footwear, stretching, and night splints.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy falls onto an outstretched hand while playing on monkey bars and presents with severe elbow pain and swelling. X-ray confirms a supracondylar humeral fracture. On exam, the radial pulse is diminished, and he has weakness of thumb and index finger flexion with decreased sensation over the palmar aspect of the lateral three and a half fingers. Which structures are most likely injured together in this classic presentation?
options: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Median nerve and brachial artery
Ulnar nerve and ulnar artery
Musculocutaneous nerve and brachial artery
Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
explanations: Incorrect — the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery are injured with proximal humeral fractures or anterior shoulder dislocation, not supracondylar elbow fractures.

Correct — the median nerve travels with the brachial artery near the elbow, and this combination is the most common neurovascular injury in pediatric supracondylar humeral fractures, explaining the diminished radial pulse and median nerve sensory/motor deficits.
Incorrect — ulnar nerve injury would cause weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles and sensory loss on the little finger side, not the thumb-side motor/sensory findings described.
Incorrect — the musculocutaneous nerve supplies the biceps and lateral forearm sensation and is not the nerve classically injured with the brachial artery in supracondylar fractures.
Incorrect — radial nerve injury above the elbow causes wrist drop and posterior arm/hand sensory loss, and its associated artery is not classically implicated in supracondylar fractures.
questions.overview: Supracondylar fracture is the most common pediatric elbow fracture, typically from a fall on an outstretched arm. The brachial artery and median nerve travel together near the fracture site and are the most commonly injured neurovascular structures, though the ulnar nerve (near the medial epicondyle) and radial nerve (wrapping laterally around the humerus) can also be affected.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with a limp and left hip pain that has progressed over several weeks. He has no history of trauma. Exam shows limited internal rotation and abduction of the left hip. Initial hip X-ray is normal. A bone scan shows decreased perfusion to the left femoral head. Which of the following best characterizes this condition?
options: Autoimmune destruction of synovium with pannus formation
Genetic mutation in FGFR3 causing impaired endochondral ossification
Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in a child, more common in males
Fracture through the femoral growth plate in an obese adolescent
Bacterial seeding of the joint requiring emergent drainage
explanations: Incorrect — this describes rheumatoid arthritis pathophysiology, not an avascular necrosis process with decreased perfusion on bone scan.
Incorrect — this describes achondroplasia, a distinct genetic skeletal dysplasia unrelated to avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

Correct — Legg-Calve-Perthes disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head occurring in children aged 4-8, more common in males (4:1), presenting with hip pain/limp and initially normal X-ray with decreased perfusion on bone scan.
Incorrect — this describes slipped capital femoral epiphysis, which occurs in obese adolescents (12-14 years), not a 6-year-old with normal initial imaging.
Incorrect — septic arthritis presents acutely with fever, marked swelling, and very high synovial WBC count, not a gradually progressive limp with normal initial X-ray.
questions.overview: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children aged 4-8 years, more common in boys, presenting with hip pain and limp. Initial X-rays are often normal, while bone scan or MRI reveals decreased femoral head perfusion early in the disease course, distinguishing it from SCFE, which occurs in older, obese adolescents.

questions.stem: Acetylcholine-mediated vasodilation of vascular smooth muscle occurs through which of the following sequences?
options: Acetylcholine directly opens L-type calcium channels on smooth muscle cells to increase contraction
Acetylcholine stimulates endothelial cells to release nitric oxide, which activates guanylyl cyclase to increase cGMP and activate myosin light chain phosphatase
Acetylcholine increases cAMP directly in smooth muscle to activate myosin light chain kinase
Acetylcholine stimulates release of RANK-L from endothelial cells to activate osteoclasts
explanations: Incorrect — acetylcholine does not directly act on smooth muscle L-type calcium channels; its vasodilatory effect requires an intact endothelium to generate nitric oxide.

Correct — acetylcholine acts indirectly on vascular smooth muscle by stimulating endothelial cells to synthesize nitric oxide (EDRF), which diffuses into smooth muscle, activates guanylyl cyclase to raise cGMP, and increases myosin light chain phosphatase activity, causing relaxation.

Incorrect — cAMP does increase in some smooth muscle relaxation pathways but inhibits, rather than activates, myosin light chain kinase; this is also not the acetylcholine-nitric oxide pathway described.
Incorrect — RANK-L/osteoclast signaling pertains to bone remodeling, unrelated to smooth muscle relaxation via nitric oxide.
questions.overview: Acetylcholine causes vasodilation indirectly by stimulating endothelial cells to synthesize nitric oxide (EDRF) from L-arginine; nitric oxide diffuses into adjacent smooth muscle cells and activates guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP levels. Increased cGMP activates myosin light chain phosphatase, dephosphorylating myosin and causing smooth muscle relaxation.

questions.stem: Muscle biopsy in a patient with proximal muscle weakness shows perimysial inflammation predominantly composed of CD4+ T-cells. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this finding?
options: Dermatomyositis
Fibromyalgia
Polymyalgia rheumatica
Polymyositis
explanations: Correct — dermatomyositis shows perimysial inflammation with CD4+ T-cells as the predominant cell type on muscle biopsy, along with characteristic skin findings such as heliotrope rash and Gottron papules.
Incorrect — fibromyalgia biopsy shows no inflammation or muscle damage, unlike the perimysial CD4+ infiltrate described.
Incorrect — polymyalgia rheumatica does not have a characteristic inflammatory myopathy biopsy pattern and does not cause true muscle weakness.
Incorrect — polymyositis shows endomysial inflammation predominantly composed of CD8+ T-cells, not the perimysial CD4+ pattern described.
questions.overview: Inflammatory myopathies are distinguished on muscle biopsy by the location and type of infiltrate: polymyositis shows endomysial inflammation with predominant CD8+ T-cells, while dermatomyositis shows perimysial inflammation with predominant CD4+ T-cells. Dermatomyositis is also distinguished clinically by pathognomonic skin findings like the heliotrope rash and Gottron papules.

questions.stem: A tennis player develops pain over the lateral elbow that worsens with resisted wrist extension. Tenderness is noted at the lateral epicondyle. Which structures classically originate at this site?
options: Pronator muscles
Wrist flexor muscles
Wrist extensor muscles
Elbow flexor muscles
explanations: Incorrect — pronator muscles (e.g., pronator teres) originate near the medial epicondyle, not the lateral epicondyle, and are unrelated to this presentation.
Incorrect — wrist flexor muscles originate at the medial epicondyle, and their overuse causes medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow), not the lateral pain described.

Correct — the lateral epicondyle is the origin of the wrist extensor muscles; overuse causes lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow), presenting with lateral elbow tenderness and pain worsened by resisted wrist extension.
Incorrect — elbow flexors (e.g., biceps, brachialis) do not originate at the lateral epicondyle and are not implicated in epicondylitis.
questions.overview: Epicondylitis is a form of chronic tendinosis from overuse, distinguished by the epicondyle involved: lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) affects the origin of wrist extensor muscles and causes pain with resisted wrist extension, while medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) affects wrist flexor origins and causes pain with resisted wrist flexion.

questions.stem: A patient undergoes pelvic surgery involving trocar placement and subsequently develops weakness of thigh adduction and numbness of the medial thigh. Which nerve was most likely injured?
options: Genitofemoral nerve
Femoral nerve
Pudendal nerve
Obturator nerve
explanations: Incorrect — genitofemoral nerve injury affects the cremasteric reflex and sensation of the anterior scrotum/thigh, not thigh adduction strength.
Incorrect — femoral nerve injury causes weak hip flexion/knee extension and an absent patellar reflex, not isolated adductor weakness and medial thigh numbness.
Incorrect — pudendal nerve injury affects perineal sensation and continence, not thigh adduction or medial thigh sensation.

Correct — the obturator nerve (L2-L4) supplies the thigh adductor muscles and sensation to the medial thigh; it courses through the posterior pelvis and is vulnerable to injury during pelvic surgery (e.g., trocar placement), causing weak adduction and medial thigh numbness.
questions.overview: The obturator nerve (L2-L4) innervates the thigh adductor muscles (adductor longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis, obturator externus) and provides sensation to the medial thigh. It courses through the posterior pelvis, making it vulnerable to injury during pelvic surgery, resulting in weak thigh adduction and medial thigh numbness.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old presents with an asymptomatic lytic lesion in the diaphysis of the femur, found incidentally. Biopsy shows irregular trabeculae of woven bone surrounded by fibrous connective tissue stroma. Which of the following best describes this condition?
options: Chondrosarcoma, a malignant tumor of chondrocytes
Fibrous dysplasia, a benign tumor of woven bone and fibroblasts
Osteosarcoma, a malignant tumor of osteoblasts
Giant cell tumor, composed of multinucleated osteoclast-like cells
explanations: Incorrect — chondrosarcoma is a malignant cartilage tumor in older adults, typically in the pelvis or proximal femur/humerus, not matching this benign adolescent diaphyseal lesion.

Correct — fibrous dysplasia is a benign bone tumor composed of woven bone surrounded by fibroblastic stroma, occurring in early adolescence in the medulla/diaphysis, often asymptomatic but capable of causing pain or fracture, and growth stops when the growth plate closes.

Incorrect — osteosarcoma is malignant, occurs in the metaphysis, shows pleomorphic cells with irregular osteoid, and classically presents with a painful enlarging mass, not the benign incidental lesion described.
Incorrect — giant cell tumor shows multinucleated giant cells in the epiphysis, not the fibrous stroma with woven bone trabeculae described in this diaphyseal lesion.
questions.overview: Fibrous dysplasia is a benign bone tumor of woven bone surrounded by fibrous connective tissue stroma, occurring in the medulla/diaphysis during early adolescence and growing until the growth plate closes. It is often asymptomatic but can cause pain or pathologic fractures, appearing as a lytic lesion in the diaphysis on X-ray.

questions.stem: A competitive swimmer develops shoulder pain with overhead activity. Exam shows pain with resisted abduction when the arms are positioned at 90 degrees of abduction and 30 degrees of forward flexion with thumbs pointing down. Which structure is most likely impinged, and between what two structures does this occur?
options: Supraspinatus tendon; between the humeral head and acromion process
Long head of biceps tendon; between the clavicle and first rib
Infraspinatus tendon; between the humeral head and coracoid process
Subscapularis tendon; between the scapula and rib cage
explanations: Correct — the supraspinatus tendon is compressed in the subacromial space between the humeral head and acromion process, producing impingement (swimmer's shoulder/thrower's shoulder); the empty can test (thumbs down) reproduces pain by increasing this impingement.
Incorrect — thoracic outlet syndrome, not biceps tendon impingement, involves compression between the clavicle and ribs; the empty/full can test specifically evaluates the supraspinatus.

Incorrect — the infraspinatus assists external rotation and is not the classic tendon compressed against the acromion in impingement syndrome, nor is the coracoid process the site of the described impingement.

Incorrect — the subscapularis mediates internal rotation and is not compressed against the rib cage; scapular winging against the rib cage relates to long thoracic nerve/serratus anterior dysfunction, not rotator cuff impingement.
questions.overview: Supraspinatus impingement is the most common rotator cuff injury, resulting from tendon compression in the subacromial space between the humeral head and acromion process, commonly seen in swimmers and throwers. The empty can test (arms abducted 90°, thumbs down) and full can test (thumbs up) help identify supraspinatus pathology, with pain suggesting tendinopathy or tear.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the structural relationship between the sarcoplasmic reticulum and T-tubules in cardiac muscle compared to skeletal muscle?
options: Both cardiac and skeletal muscle form triads with two terminal cisternae per T-tubule
Cardiac muscle forms dyads (one T-tubule with one terminal cisterna), while skeletal muscle forms triads (one T-tubule with two terminal cisternae)
Cardiac muscle forms triads, while skeletal muscle forms dyads
Neither cardiac nor skeletal muscle contains specialized T-tubule/SR junctions
explanations: Incorrect — only skeletal muscle forms triads with two terminal cisternae per T-tubule; cardiac muscle has the simpler dyad arrangement.

Correct — cardiac muscle has a less extensive sarcoplasmic reticulum and forms dyads (one T-tubule paired with one terminal cisterna), whereas skeletal muscle forms triads (one T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae).
Incorrect — this reverses the correct pairing; dyads are characteristic of cardiac muscle, and triads are characteristic of skeletal muscle.
Incorrect — both muscle types have specialized T-tubule/SR junctions essential for excitation-contraction coupling, just with different structural arrangements (dyads vs. triads).
questions.overview: Cardiac and skeletal muscle share sarcomeric structure but differ in their T-tubule/sarcoplasmic reticulum arrangement: cardiac muscle has a less extensive SR forming dyads (one T-tubule with one terminal cisterna), while skeletal muscle forms triads (one T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae). Cardiac muscle also uniquely depends on extracellular calcium influx through L-type channels to trigger calcium-induced calcium release during phase 2 of its action potential.
